blocks.text: Transition elements form complex ions because they have vacant d orbitals that are low enough in energy (energetically accessible) to accept electron pairs. A central ion such as Fe3+ or Cu2+ has partly filled or empty (n-1)d orbitals that accept lone pairs from ligands, forming coordinate (dative) bonds: for example Cu2+(aq) + 4NH3(aq) -> [Cu(NH3)4]2+.

blocks.alt: Cu2+(aq) + 4NH3(aq) gives a complex drawn as Cu (charge 2+) in the centre with four NH3 molecules at the corners of a square, each joined by an arrow pointing from N to Cu, all inside square brackets with charge 2+.
blocks.caption: Formation of the [Cu(NH3)4]2+ complex ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered scheme).

blocks.title: Complex and ligand
blocks.text: A complex (coordination compound) is a molecule or ion formed by a central metal atom or ion surrounded by one or more ligands. A ligand is a molecule or ion with at least one lone pair that forms a dative covalent bond to the central metal atom or ion. The metal acts as a Lewis acid (electron-pair acceptor) and the ligand as a Lewis base (electron-pair donor); the word comes from the Latin ligare, to bind.

items: Anionic ligands (the most common): Cl-, CN-, OH-, C2O4 2-. Their names end in -o: chloride becomes chloro, cyanide cyano.
Neutral ligands: H2O, NH3, CO. Most keep their names, but some have special ones: H2O is aqua, NH3 ammine and CO carbonyl.
Cationic ligands are rare; their names often end in -ium, e.g. NO+ (nitrosonium) and NH2-NH3+ (hydrazinium).

blocks.text: Kinds of ligand by number of donor atoms

items: Monodentate: donates only one pair of electrons, through a single atom, e.g. H2O, NH3, CO, Cl-, OH- and CN-.

Bidentate: donates two electron pairs, e.g. 1,2-diaminoethane (ethylenediamine, H2NCH2CH2NH2, written en), where each N atom gives a lone pair, and the ethanedioate (oxalate) ion C2O4 2-, where one O atom of each carboxylate group does.
Polydentate: forms more than two dative bonds to one metal ion. EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetate) is hexadentate: it binds through six donor atoms, two N and four O.

blocks.alt: Displayed formulas of three ligands: 1,2-diaminoethane (H2N-CH2-CH2-NH2), ethanedioate (two C atoms joined, each with one C=O and one O-) and ethylenediaminetetraacetate, EDTA (two N atoms, each with a lone pair, joined by CH2-CH2 and each carrying two CH2-COO- arms).
blocks.caption: Structures of 1,2-diaminoethane, ethanedioate and ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA) (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered structures).

blocks.title: Coordination number and coordination sphere
blocks.text: The coordination number is the total number of dative bonds between the ligands and the central metal atom or ion. The coordination sphere is the central metal with its directly bonded ligands, written inside square brackets. Its charge is the sum of the charges of the metal ion and the ligands; the metal's charge is the sphere's charge minus the ligands' total charge.

blocks.alt: [Fe(CN)6]4-: Fe (charge 2+) in the centre with six CN ligands, each joined by an arrow pointing to Fe, in square brackets with charge 4-. A bracket 'In this complex' lists: central metal ion = Fe2+; ligand = CN-; coordination number = 6; total charge of ligands = -6; charge on metal = +2; charge on coordination sphere = -4.
